Nowhere did I find a really clear space for sketching until this occasion when I prolonged beyond the proper limit the process of lying on my back in bed. Then the light of that white heaven broke upon my vision, that breadth of mere white which is indeed almost the definition of Paradise, since it means purity and also means freedom. But alas! like all heavens, now that it is seen it is found to be unattainable; it looks more austere and more distant than the blue sky outside the window. For my proposal to paint on it with the bristly end of a broom has been discouraged—never mind by whom; by a person debarred from all political rights—and even my minor proposal to put the other end of the broom into the kitchen fire and turn it to charcoal has not been conceded. Yet I am certain that it was from persons in my position that all the original inspiration came for covering the ceilings of palaces and cathedrals with a riot of fallen angels or victorious gods. I am sure that it was only because Michael Angelo was engaged in the ancient and honourable occupation of lying in bed that he ever realized how the roof of the Sistine Chapel might be made into an awful imitation of a divine drama that could only be acted in the heavens.

The tone now commonly taken toward the practice of lying in bed is hypocritical and unhealthy. Of all the marks of modernity that seem to mean a kind of decadence, there is none more menacing and dangerous than the exultation of very small and secondary matters of conduct at the expense of very great and primary ones, at the expense of eternal ties and tragic human morality. If there is one thing worse than the modern weakening of major morals, it is the modern strengthening of minor morals. Thus it is considered more withering to accuse a man of bad taste than of bad ethics. Cleanliness is not next to godliness nowadays, for cleanliness is made essential and godliness is regarded as an offence. A playwright can attack the institution of marriage so long as he does not misrepresent the manners of society, and I have met Ibsenite pessimists who thought it wrong to take beer but right to take prussic acid. Especially this is so in matters of hygiene; notably such matters as lying in bed. Instead of being regarded, as it ought to be, as a matter of personal convenience and adjustment, it has come to be regarded by many as if it were a part of essential morals to get up early in the morning. It is upon the whole part of practical wisdom; but there is nothing good about it or bad about its opposite.

message.content:
I struggled to find a truly open space for sketching until that moment when I extended my time lying supine in bed beyond the usual limit. At that moment, the brilliance of a pure white expanse illuminated my sight, a vastness that could almost be described as Paradise, embodying both purity and freedom. However, as is often the case with such celestial visions, once it is perceived, it appears even more forbidding and remote than the azure sky outside my window. My whimsical idea of using the coarse tip of a broom to paint on this heavenly canvas was swiftly discouraged—by someone who, notably, has no political rights—and even my less ambitious thought of igniting the other end of the broom to create charcoal was denied. Yet, I am convinced that those of us who share my predicament were the very source of initial inspiration for adorning the ceilings of grand palaces and cathedrals with chaotic depictions of fallen angels or triumphant deities. Surely, it was through the act of reclining that Michelangelo conceived the profound vision of transforming the Sistine Chapel's ceiling into a grand yet flawed representation of a divine narrative meant to take place in the heavens.

The contemporary attitude towards the act of lying in bed is fraught with hypocrisy and is quite detrimental. Among the signs of modernity that seem to evoke a sense of decline, none is more alarming than the glorification of trivial and secondary behavioral norms at the expense of significant and fundamental moral principles—those that involve eternal bonds and the weight of human ethics. If there’s anything more troubling than the contemporary erosion of substantial morals, it is the paradoxical reinforcement of minor ones. Today, it is deemed more scathing to label someone as having poor taste than to accuse them of unethical behavior. Cleanliness, which once was said to be close to divinity, has now been elevated to a necessity, while spirituality is often dismissed as an affront. A playwright may criticize the sanctity of marriage as long as they remain true to societal conventions, and I have encountered Ibsenite pessimists who believe it wrong to drink beer while considering it acceptable to consume prussic acid. This trend is particularly evident in discussions surrounding hygiene, especially when it comes to the act of lying in bed. Rather than being viewed as a matter of personal comfort and adaptability, it is increasingly perceived by many as a moral imperative to rise early each day. While it may be a component of practical wisdom, there is nothing inherently virtuous or sinful about it or its contrary.
